doc.title: Charles Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Checker cabs to Rudy Van Gelder's studio and the microphone secret
summary: Rehearsal came a day or two before; everyone rode cabs to the studio, with no headphones, a horseshoe setup and Van Gelder's Schoeps microphones to two-track master.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: So on that day you described a rehearsal and then getting into a taxi and going to Van Gelder’s studios. So am I correct that that whole record was rehearsed and recorded in one day?

No. There was one day, maybe two, depending on the complexity of the songs. And then the next day everybody would file into a couple of Checker cabs. I guess if you had a Checker cab now it would be worth something on the antique car market you know.
Right. A lot of that is being —
With the little jumper seats facing the regular seats, you know, so you could get luggage in there, you could get three, four, maybe five passengers, two facing the other three.
And a saxophone and a trumpet.
Yeah all of that in the trunk and off we’d go. And that was the procedure for any Blue Note recording, other than, you know, musicians who had their own cars. They would drive to Rudy’s studio.
Did you wear headphones at that point? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Yeah, there wasn’t a practice of wearing earphones. I mean I suppose they were in use but I don’t recall any use of headphones. They were all in a sort of semi horseshoe set up, the piano the farthest away, and then bass and drums right together, no partitions or anything. And the horns facing the piano. So it was sort of like a little J type of thing. But the secret of Rudy Van Gelder was his microphones.
Well he was using French Schoeps and special coverings for them, and a direct-to-master two track.
But it was how he equalized everything coming in you know.
